output.answer: Somali-Canadian sisters Iman and Siham Hashi, known collectively as Faarrow, are recording their debut album in Los Angeles. Born in Mogadishu, they fled to Canada as refugees in 1991 following the outbreak of war. Now based in LA via Atlanta, the duo is preparing to release an Afro-pop sound described as a fusion of pop, hip-hop, and rhythmic African percussion. Their album, largely written and produced by the sisters alongside actor-musician Elijah Kelley, is currently in the mixing phase under Warner Brothers Records. Influenced by artists like Michael Jackson and the Spice Girls, Faarrow combines their musical career with significant humanitarian efforts. Working as spokespersons for the UNHCR, they advocate for refugees, having headlined events at the Kennedy Center and the Nansen Awards. Additionally, they launched "Wish Creatively," a socially conscious fashion brand selling jewelry to fund sustainable income projects for women in Kenya and Somalia. The sisters view their success as a way to inspire their generation, proving that creative paths can effectively contribute to rebuilding Somalia without conforming to traditional expectations.

Somali-Canadian sisters Iman, 25, and Siham Hashi, 27, known collectively as Faarrow, are finalizing their debut album in Los Angeles. Born in Mogadishu, they fled to Canada as refugees in 1991 after war broke out, later discovering a passion for music influenced by artists like Michael Jackson and the Spice Girls. Their upcoming album, largely written and produced by the sisters alongside actor-musician Elijah Kelley, features a fusion sound blending pop, hip-hop, and rhythmic African percussion. Signed to Warner Brothers Records, the duo is currently in the mixing process with plans to release their first single soon. Beyond music, Faarrow serves as UNHCR spokespersons, advocating for refugees through social media and benefit concerts. They also founded "Wish Creatively," a socially conscious fashion brand selling jewelry to fund sustainable income projects for women in Kenya and Somalia. The sisters view their creative success as a way to inspire their generation and support Somalia's rebuilding without conforming to traditional expectations that undervalue artistic careers.

output.answer: Former Australia cricket captain and legendary broadcaster Richie Benaud has died at the age of 84. Recently treated for skin cancer, Benaud was described by Cricket Australia as the most famous Australian player after Don Bradman. A veteran of 64 Test matches, he was a record-breaking leg-spinner who never lost a series in his 28 Tests as captain. Inducted into the Sport Australia Hall of Fame in 1985, he spent over four decades with the BBC, becoming the voice of cricket for millions in Britain and Australia. His passing triggered global condolences, including from Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott, who ordered flags flown at half-mast, and British Prime Minister David Cameron. Tributes poured in from cricket legends like Shane Warne, who called him a mentor and "godfather of cricket," and Michael Clarke. Writers and peers praised his authoritative yet dignified commentary style, noting he set incredibly high standards both on and off the field. Born in 1930 in Penrith, New South Wales, Benaud remains an iconic figure who defined an era of the sport.

Former Australia cricket captain and legendary broadcaster Richie Benaud has died at the age of 84. Recently treated for skin cancer, Benaud was described by Cricket Australia as the most famous Australian player after Don Bradman. output.answer: In Nepal's Kavre District, the earthquake's magnitude is evident in cracked highways east of Kathmandu, where fissures are filled with rubble to allow passage. The 30-kilometer journey to Ravi Opi now takes two hours. While relatively lucky compared to areas closer to the epicenter, 90% of houses in Ravi Opi are uninhabitable, with residents fearing aftershocks. Maili Tamang, 62, survived after her two-story home collapsed, injuring her leg; her daughter-in-law was transported by motorbike to a distant missionary hospital. Mahesh Koiraba lost his two-year-old daughter, Prati, digging through wreckage with his hands. Despite small landslides and locals clearing roads, little aid has arrived. Displaced families, including Osminda Koirale's group, huddle in makeshift shelters without government support, lacking food and clothes. Torrential rain and powerful overnight aftershocks have heightened fear and hampered recovery. While this region is only 90 minutes from the capital, remote villages reachable only on foot were hit hardest, with unknown human losses and no aid yet delivered.

output.answer: Millennials are increasingly prioritizing careers, travel, and financial stability over traditional marriage, potentially signaling a 'marriage apocalypse.' Journalism students from Kent State University expressed that they will marry only on their own terms, viewing weddings as expensive distractions from experiences like traveling to Europe. They prefer being single and successful rather than unhappy in relationships driven by fear of loneliness. This shift reflects a culture shaped by rising divorce rates; the number of US adults who have been married more than once has risen from 14 million in 1960 to nearly 42 million today. A Pew Research report indicates half of respondents believe society is fine without marriage priorities, a view held by two-thirds of young adults. While economists note marriage correlates with economic well-being, many millennials delay union due to personal debt and a desire for debt-free partners. Comparisons to Scandinavia show high cohabitation and out-of-wedlock birth rates alongside top quality-of-life rankings, suggesting marriage isn't essential for societal success. Swedes cite lack of legal advantages and secular values as reasons to avoid formal marriage. Ultimately, while the author found commitment valuable for navigating life's challenges, the trend suggests marriage is becoming a choice based purely on love and practicality rather than social expectation.

output.answer: Millennials are increasingly delaying or rejecting marriage to prioritize careers, travel, and financial stability. Kent State journalism students told the author they view weddings as expensive distractions; 21-year-old Jackie Demate prefers spending $20,000 on Europe, while Candace Monacelli emphasizes using her degree for success rather than motherhood. Debt also hinders plans, with student Emily Crille noting it is hard to plan a wedding while owing thousands. This shift reflects a culture rich in divorce; U.S. remarriages rose from 14 million in 1960 to 42 million recently. A Pew Research report indicates 50% of respondents believe society is fine without marriage, including 66% of adults aged 18-29. While economists link marriage to economic well-being, causality remains unclear. The article contrasts this with Scandinavia, where cohabitation is common and out-of-wedlock births are high, yet quality-of-life rankings remain top-tier. Swedes cite lack of legal advantages and secular values as reasons for avoiding marriage. Ultimately, these young adults view marriage as strictly about love, not obligation. The author, a child of divorce who married at 38, acknowledges the validity of both single life and committed partnerships, leaving open whether a marriage-free society would be equally well-off.

To attach multiple picture frames together, you can use a couple of methods. One way is to use a stand grouping method where you select two or three frames of the same wood molding. For joining two frames, use identical frames. If you're joining three together, choose either three of the same or one which is larger to be the middle frame. Lay them beside each other to check the effect. Put two frames together back to back, and mark the hinge placement. The placement should be the same distance from the bottom edges of each frame to ensure that the grouped pictures stand securely on the table top. Attach two small hinges to the connecting sides of the frames. 

Another method involves screwing the frame to a backer board. Repeat this with each frame. Have the pictures all ready in the frames to save time. You can always unscrew them at a later date to change the picture if you want. Attach a hanging wire to the back, hang it up and step back to enjoy the results. 

If you're hanging multiple pictures together, it may be helpful to test ideas by laying the group of pictures out on the floor first.

To attach multiple picture frames together, you can use a couple of methods. One way is to use a stand grouping method where you select two or three frames of the same wood molding. For joining two frames, use identical frames. If you're joining three together, choose either three of the same or one which is larger to be the middle frame. Lay them beside each other to check the effect. Put two frames together back to back, and mark the hinge placement. The placement should be the same distance from the bottom edges of each frame to ensure that the grouped pictures stand securely on the table top. Attach two small hinges to the connecting sides of the frames. 

Another method involves screwing the frame to a backer board. Repeat this with each frame. Have the pictures all ready in the frames to save time. You can always unscrew them at a later date to change the picture if you want. Attach a hanging wire to the back, hang it up and step back to enjoy the results. 

If you're hanging multiple pictures together, it may be helpful to test ideas by laying the group of pictures out on the floor first.

Based on the provided passages, the main difference between ad hominem fallacy and poisoning the well fallacy is the timing of the attack.

Ad hominem fallacy occurs when an attack is made on a person's character, motive, or other attribute directly related to their argument, rather than attacking the argument itself. This type of attack can happen at any point during a debate or discussion.

On the other hand, poisoning the well fallacy involves making an ad hominem attack (i.e., attacking a person's character or integrity) before the merits of a case can be considered. In other words, it is an attempt to discredit a person's argument by attacking their personal integrity or intelligence before the discussion has even begun.

So, while both fallacies involve attacking a person's character rather than their argument, ad hominem fallacy happens after the argument has been presented, while poisoning the well fallacy happens before the argument is even presented.

Based on the provided passages, the main difference between ad hominem fallacy and poisoning the well fallacy is the timing of the attack.

Ad hominem fallacy occurs when an attack is made on a person's character, motive, or other attribute directly related to their argument, rather than attacking the argument itself. This type of attack can happen at any point during a debate or discussion.

On the other hand, poisoning the well fallacy involves making an ad hominem attack (i.e., attacking a person's character or integrity) before the merits of a case can be considered. In other words, it is an attempt to discredit a person's argument by attacking their personal integrity or intelligence before the discussion has even begun.

So, while both fallacies involve attacking a person's character rather than their argument, ad hominem fallacy happens after the argument has been presented, while poisoning the well fallacy happens before the argument is even presented.
